item.title: PamStealer Targets macOS as Silent Push Details Proactive Phishing Infrastructure Hunting
item.content:encoded:
PamStealer Uses Fake Maccy Sites and PAM Checks to Steal Mac Login Passwords — Should Read

Researchers found a new macOS infostealer, PamStealer, spread through fake Maccy websites that tricks users into running a malicious AppleScript and then steals passwords, browser data, crypto wallet data, iCloud Keychain content, and clipboard contents. Its key tactic is validating the victim’s macOS login password locally through PAM before exfiltrating data, making the credential theft more reliable and stealthy.

  • Jamf Threat Labs discovered a new macOS information stealer called PamStealer that is distributed as a compiled AppleScript file impersonating the legitimate open-source clipboard manager Maccy.
  • PamStealer is delivered through a lookalike website, maccyapp.com, that mimics the official Maccy website at maccy.app.
  • The malware uses a two-stage chain in which an AppleScript inside a disk image downloads a Rust-based information stealer capable of credential theft, browser data collection, persistence, and exfiltration.
  • The AppleScript dropper only continues after fingerprinting the host, including CPU architecture, locale, keyboard layout, and time zone, and it avoids Intel-based Macs, sandboxed or analysis environments, and systems associated with several Eastern European countries.
  • The Rust payload steals data from web browsers, cryptocurrency wallet extensions, iCloud Keychain, and clipboard content, and it uses a native password prompt to capture and validate the victim’s macOS login password through the PAM API.

Powerful Pivots: Hunting with Infrastructure Fingerprints — Optional

Silent Push demonstrates how defenders can find related phishing sites by pivoting on shared infrastructure fingerprints like HTTP Hash and JARM instead of changing domain names or page content. The example shows these fingerprints linking a Harbor Freight-themed phishing domain to other high-confidence phishing infrastructure such as gmaii.email.

  • The article says threat actors often reuse the same server configurations even when hosting different campaigns.
  • A phishing domain, harborfrieght[.]shop, was identified as an example for extracting a server’s unique technical signatures.
  • The article identifies HHV f2bbb45599ecd7349b164c98a8 and JARM 27d40d40d00040d00042d43d00041df04c41293ba84f6efe3a613b22f983e6 as key indicators for pivoting.
  • The goal of the technique is to find all domains hosted on infrastructure with the exact same HHV and JARM fingerprints.
  • The article says this multi-layered search identifies high-fidelity phishing sites such as gmaii.email while ignoring legitimate Google infrastructure.

Powerful Pivots: From a Single Phish to a Full Campaign — Optional

A single Ledger phishing email can be used as a starting point to uncover a broader campaign by pivoting from headers, links, page titles, domain patterns, WHOIS data, and registrars. The key takeaway is to turn reactive phishing investigations into proactive hunts for related infrastructure before it is used.

  • The article uses a real-world “Ledger” phishing email to show how a reactive investigation can become a proactive hunt.
  • The investigation begins with email headers and identifies IPs such as 149.72.223.116 and 159.183.183.61 as indicators of compromised SendGrid accounts.
  • The malicious link in the phishing email was ledger-recovery-app.com.
  • The article describes using the domain as a pivot to find other sites with an HTML title of “Are you human?” and a URL containing “ledger.”
  • The article describes a proactive domain query for ledger-*-*.com or *-ledger-*.com domains registered through Amazon Registrar, Inc. to find domains when they are registered before they are used in an email campaign.

Staying "Left of Boom" with Preemptive Cyber Defense — Optional

Silent Push’s webinar explains how security teams can stay “left of boom” by monitoring static and change data to identify attacker infrastructure before it is used in campaigns. The key takeaway is that proactive tracking of DNS and infrastructure changes can give defenders earlier warning of emerging threats.

  • Senior Threat Researcher Zach Edwards explains how to stay “left of boom” with proactive cyber defence.
  • The session says organizations can identify attacker infrastructure before it is weaponized by tracking both static data and change data.
  • The article covers the difference between static data and change data in threat detection.
  • The article discusses how threat actors adapt to evade detection and how fingerprinting attacker infrastructure can help spot emerging campaigns.
  • The session covers monitoring DNS and infrastructure changes for early warning, along with tools and strategies for proactive threat hunting.

Get Started with Silent Push Community Edition — Optional

Silent Push is promoting its free Community Edition, which offers introductory access to its cyber defense platform and datasets for investigating relationships across Internet infrastructure.

  • Silent Push Community Edition is a free cyber defense tool that provides introductory access to the Silent Push platform and datasets.
  • Researchers use Silent Push to uncover relationships between billions of Internet datapoints.
  • The platform helps expose how adversaries deploy and manage their infrastructure.
  • Silent Push invites users to sign up for the Community Edition for free and provide feedback.
